A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenVid-1M, OpenVidHD-0.4M, and MVDiT work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and inspecting v2's embedded visual examples.

before.justification: v2 reports original dataset statistics, text-to-video evaluations, qualitative comparisons, and controlled ablations in Figures 3–8 and Tables 2–5.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and adds restoration results, module ablations, human caption evaluations, and an inference-acceleration analysis.

M1.justification: The core curation pipeline and MVDiT architecture remain unchanged. However, v3 Appendix C introduces an inference procedure that caches and reuses attention and feedforward outputs on alternating denoising steps without retraining. Expanded descriptions of filtering and MVDiT otherwise document existing components.

E1.justification: v3 extends evaluation beyond text-to-video generation to arbitrary-resolution video restoration, including a low-resolution UDM10 example in Figure 7, and adds direct human assessment of caption quality. Existing generation coverage remains; Panda-50M-HD is a resolution-selected subset of previously used data.

E2.justification: Relative to v2 Table 2, v3 Table 3 adds CogVideoX-5B and replaces OpenSoraPlan-V1.1 with V1.2 in the quantitative comparison; V1.1 remains in qualitative figures. The restoration experiment introduces Upscale-A-Video as a comparator. The earlier qualitative comparison against Gen2 is removed.

E3.justification: v3 adds a native-HD Panda training control, restoration training using approximately 130K synthesized samples with fidelity, perceptual, and temporal metrics, and a caption study covering 1,117 samples and 10 volunteers using four five-point criteria and preferences. These introduce substantial evaluation designs; the retained 700-prompt generation benchmark and existing 50K-step controls remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 Table 7 adds MHCA and scaling-parameter ablations, with a further reported failure when MMTA is removed. Caption-error assessment and attention-redundancy/caching analyses add new diagnostic evidence. Existing resolution, architecture, and training-data ablations remain in Table 6; v2's filtering ablation moves unchanged from Table 5 to v3 Table 9.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v3's caption-rating means and preference percentages remain point estimates; the volunteer count describes study size rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained generation scores are unchanged, including Ours at 73.46 VQAA and 68.58 VQAT. Adding CogVideoX-5B at 76.86 VQAT changes the latter ranking to second. New results include the native-HD Panda control, restoration and module-ablation scores, 80.75% preference for generated captions, up to 1.7× inference acceleration, and replacement qualitative examples.

T1.justification: The MVDiT mathematical formulation is retained, with v2 Equations 3–4 combined into v3 Equation 3 and subsequent renumbering. No substantive theorem, proof, formal assumption, or derivation is added. The caching discussion's standard quadratic-attention complexity statement is explanatory.

C1.justification: The dataset and MVDiT contributions persist, but v3's introduction makes superiority on video restoration an explicit third contribution. This substantially extends the claimed usefulness beyond v2's text-to-video-focused contributions. The motivation also shifts from manageable dataset size toward maintaining million-scale coverage with better videos and captions.

C2.justification: The central quality and alignment interpretations remain. v3 adds explanations of caching redundancy and restoration benefits, and acknowledges caption hallucinations and remaining motion-description weaknesses. Its limitations remove the explicit inability to model long-duration dynamics and add a hypothesis that more high-quality training data could improve physical realism.

D1.justification: v3 Table 1 adds GPU counts and processing times; Appendix A.1 details scoring, three cascaded cut detectors, and human-guided filtering thresholds; Section 6.1 expands staged-resolution training documentation. Conversely, v2's hosting, CC-BY-4.0 licensing, maintenance discussion, and frozen-encoder statement disappear. These are documentation changes, not evidence that access or encoder training actually changed.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for CogVideoX, Upscale-A-Video, DeepCache, and the restoration example's source. Appendix A.2 expands the relationship to MMDiT, and Section 5 explicitly asserts priority for the parallel visual-text structure in video generation. The dedicated OpenSora pipeline comparison is removed, while the broader related-work positioning remains.

P1.justification: v3 revises and condenses introductory, related-work, curation, and method prose, updates conference front matter and citation style, and reorganizes the appendices. The dataset overview moves into Section 4 and filtering ablations move to Appendix B. The main section sequence and substantial portions of the scientific exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the opening mosaic with a dataset comparison, replaces earlier animated comparison panels with different examples displayed as frame sequences, and adds restoration, filtering, caching, and duration graphics. Tables gain resource and duration columns and new experimental displays. Figures 13–15 enlarge Figure 6's existing examples rather than adding independent comparisons.

improvement.justification: v2 supported caption quality largely through length statistics and compared HD training chiefly against upsampled outputs. v3's human caption study, native-HD Panda control, and component ablations substantially strengthen evidence for the central dataset and model claims; processing details also improve auditability. Removing licensing information and the long-duration limitation weakens transparency, and the restoration comparison does not isolate dataset effects. Nevertheless, the stronger evidence addressing important gaps supports a substantial net improvement.
